ai_summary:
Scotland’s renewable energy output remains robust, with estimated Scottish wind output reaching 4.9 GW, representing 48.5% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Across the wider system, total GB wind output stands at 13.7 GW. This strong volume of regional clean generation keeps Scottish carbon intensity at 0 gCO2/kWh, standing in stark contrast to the GB-wide carbon intensity of 128 gCO2/kWh. 

Nevertheless, critical grid infrastructure bottlenecks continue to restrict the optimal transfer of this zero-carbon electricity southward. As a consequence, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has accumulated to 40483.3 MWh, incurring an economic constraint cost of about £1,020,558. The operational repercussions extend directly to system decarbonisation targets; because clean power cannot flow freely across transmission boundaries, thermal plants must ramp up downstream. The estimated gas burned elsewhere to replace it has reached 7691827.0 m3, releasing an unnecessary 14169.2 tonnes CO2 into the atmosphere. These figures demonstrate the ongoing dilemma of network bottlenecks, which force the suppression of abundant zero-carbon generation while driving up balancing expenses and national emissions.
